name: Edward Lambert
age: 53 (weathered to read as 60s — 'the last eleven years added the decade that the previous forty-two had not')
body: middling height — neither commanding a room by stature nor overlooked by it; frame lean but not gaunt, once solidly built in the northern-frontier manner (broad enough through chest and shoulders to carry armour and swing a blade competently), now thinned by eleven years of stress the appetite never replaced; long angular face weathered like old leather, deep-set iron-grey eyes shadowed by a heavy brow, close-cropped grey-brown hair, clean-shaven, dressed always in plain dark wool that says means without display
energy: low and contained, the same even keel whether he is reciting a grain count or ordering hostages killed — control is the whole performance; the one time he is pushed past it (the hostage order) the voice does not rise, it just empties out
register: formal, clipped, bureaucratic-administrative; near-zero contractions, numbers cited like a ledger (years, four, eleven, three), dry self-aware irony rather than warmth, no rhetorical flourish because he considers persuasion-by-inflection a form of dishonesty

Lambert let the silence sit for three full seconds, which was his way of declining to be hurried.
Lambert did not raise his voice at all.
Lambert's voice did not change register at all, which was how everyone at that table understood he had stopped being agreeable.
"Be frugal," Lambert said. "In grain, in coin, and in the number of people you tell they are wrong. All three ledgers run out."

"Your highness." Lambert set the hand flat on his knee. "I have written four letters to the Ore Council in eleven years. I have received three replies. All three were courteous. None of them contained a fact."

reference_direction: An older male voice, medium-low and dry, running at an almost perfectly even pace with very little pitch inflection — the vocal equivalent of a well-oiled mechanism, not a warm one. No softness, no rasp of effort, only the faint papery wear of age at the edges. Formal register, no contractions, numbers delivered like citations. Comparison: picture a meticulous frontier estate-steward or quartermaster reading a ledger aloud to a room he already knows is listening — never needs volume to be obeyed, and the one time the content turns horrifying (ordering hostages killed) the voice doesn't rise, it just goes emptier, which is the more frightening choice.
one_line: A dry, even, medium-low administrator's voice that never once raises in eleven years — control itself is the performance, and horror reads as the voice going flatter, not louder.
